items.articleText: formafantasma on research, design, and the exhibition space , the Milan- and Rotterdam-based studio founded by Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, exhibition design starts with looking closely at the relationship between the artworks, the building, the institution, and the people moving through it. The duo’s research-driven practice often looks at materials, culture, and the relationship between tradition and contemporary production, and they bring the same curiosity to exhibition-making. They look for what they call ‘the tension’ in a project — the moments when the artworks, architecture, curatorial idea, and established ways of displaying art don’t quite line up. ‘There is no fixed methodology, because exhibition design is always relational,’ Formafantasma tells designboom Research and design happen at the same time in the duo’s process. The studio looks at the artworks, their material and historical context, the building they will be shown in, and the conventions of display, while also testing walls, materials, sightlines, and other ways of organizing the space. Sometimes, a seemingly pragmatic decision can reveal the larger question. ‘An apparently pragmatic decision, a wall, a fabric, a particular sightline, reveals a conceptual question that becomes central to the project,’ The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum challenging the supposedly neutral exhibition space That way of working also leads Formafantasma to question one of the most familiar conventions of contemporary exhibition-making: neutrality. The white cube can appear to disappear around an artwork, but the studio argues that its familiarity does not make it neutral. ‘A white plaster wall is no less designed than a metal or textile wall,’ ‘It has simply become so familiar within contemporary art that we have stopped seeing it as a choice.’ Their exhibitions of Caravaggio and Bernini at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam and Mike Kelley at Moderna Museet show how they approach this idea differently depending on the work. For Caravaggio and Bernini, they moved away from the darkness and theatrical lighting associated with the artists, using an exhibition language closer to the white cube. With Mike Kelley, they did almost the opposite, bringing the industrial character of the museum into the foreground through metal panels. In both cases, the architecture around the works is treated as part of the exhibition and not as something that fades into the background. ‘The response therefore cannot precede the question,’ Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin explain . ‘It emerges from looking very closely at what is already there.’ For the studio, the objective is to identify the particular spatial conditions that might make relationships within each project more visible or more complicated. ‘We are less interested in finding a visual language that will unify everything than in understanding what spatial condition might make the relationships within an exhibition more legible or more complex,’ shares with designboom. This also explains their interest in the history of display itself. The way objects are exhibited is never simply a technical matter. ‘We have become increasingly interested in the exhibition itself as an object of inquiry: why a wall looks the way it does, why information occupies a particular position, why visitors are expected to move or sit in particular ways, why some materials appear neutral while others become immediately visible,’ The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum turning curatorial ideas into spatial conditions This relationship between concept and physical space is evident in Formafantasma’s work for the 2026 Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale. Curators Nora Razian and Sabih Ahmed were thinking about movement, migration, oral transmission, and different forms of passage. The Biennale’s setting in the JAX district, meanwhile, consisted of very large industrial spaces. Formafantasma introduced porous textile partitions and wooden structures that established boundaries without severing one space from another. Visitors could often perceive another work, room, or presence through the architecture. ‘The curatorial idea of movement therefore wasn’t represented symbolically; it began to affect how boundaries themselves behaved,’ the studio highlights. Instead of translating a curatorial idea into an obvious visual metaphor, Formafantasma allows it to influence the physical organization of the exhibition. The conceptual and the practical develop alongside one another, a process that applies to questions that might initially appear purely technical, such as whether a work can tolerate daylight, how much acoustic separation a sound work requires, what should be visible behind an artwork, where visitors can rest, and how much material should be introduced for an exhibition that will exist for only a few months. ‘Conceptual questions and technical questions are not separate for us,’ ‘The exhibition emerges through their negotiation.’ The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Martin Schgaguler, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum providing structure without prescribing interpretation Visitor movement is another area where Formafantasma resists the idea of complete control. Sightlines, thresholds, concealment, and revelation can all affect what becomes visible and when, but the studio is wary of treating an exhibition as a choreography in which every visitor follows an intended sequence. ‘We would resist thinking of movement as something we can completely choreograph,’ ‘Choreography can imply that the designer knows how the visitor should move and what they should experience at each moment. We are more interested in establishing conditions and possibilities.’ The approach changes according to context. At the Venice Biennale, where visitors encounter a high density of artworks and information, directing the gaze and creating moments of visual relief can become important. In a smaller exhibition, there may be greater room for wandering and ambiguity. For House of Nisaba: New Stories of Painting, curated by Hendrik Folkerts at Moderna Museet in 2026, Formafantasma deliberately avoided a central axis and prescribed sequence. From outside, the exhibition appears as a single architectural object. Inside, that unity fragmented into multiple routes and views created by straight and curved cardboard partitions. The architecture gave visitors orientation without establishing one narrative. ‘Perhaps the distinction is between providing a structure and prescribing an interpretation,’ ‘A structure can be precise while remaining open to other readings.’ The choice of cardboard sharpened this idea further. At a distance, the architecture could appear almost monumental, with a clear perimeter and threshold. Up close, however, the material was visibly fragile and provisional. ‘We liked that contradiction,’ ‘It was almost a cathedral made from cardboard: monumental but open to revision.’ Despite its monumental scale, the material could be cut, moved, and rebuilt, making the space feel more like a full-scale model. Eccentrica at Centro Pecci | image by Marco Cappelletti the artwork and its temporary ecology Formafantasma describes this relationship between artwork and setting through an unexpected analogy: a nature documentary. ‘There is an animal in the foreground, which we understand to be the protagonist, and behind it there is a landscape that we somehow perceive as scenery,’ ‘Ecologically, of course, this distinction makes no sense. The animal exists through its relationships with that environment.’ The same, they argue, is true of an exhibition. Artwork, architecture, neighboring works, texts, light, materials, visitors, and the institution form a ‘temporary ecology.’ Changing one element changes the relationships between the others. This is why the studio rejects the idea of exhibition architecture as a passive background. Its role is to acknowledge that the conditions of display are already active. One of the projects that most clearly shifted Formafantasma’s understanding of this possibility was Oltre Terra, an exhibition that the duo both curated and designed. Investigating wool and the complicated relationships between humans, sheep, landscapes, agriculture, and extraction, the project also examined the history of the diorama as a device for isolating, reconstructing, and observing nature. Because Formafantasma was responsible for both the research and the exhibition apparatus, display could become part of the investigation. ‘The distinction between content and display became much less useful,’ The project helped the studio understand that exhibition design could do more than contain research. It could articulate an argument. That position places Formafantasma’s exhibition work within the broader logic of their practice, which moves between research, materials, objects, and users. The team uses the act of designing to expose the systems and conventions that shape what we encounter. ‘The conventions of exhibiting are extraordinarily powerful precisely because most of the time we Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times . The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems. Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Hawkins is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State. Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023. Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge ’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on. It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years . That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs. All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed. The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring. GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder , GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement , clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.” Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years: And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live. GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone. CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect . They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices. So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring. items.articleText: ‘le bruit du bois’ makes a pavilion you can play High above Faverges-Seythenex in the French Alps structure cuts across the grassy slope. It is a pavilion , but its architecture comes with a second use. Visitors can pick up a wooden stick and play it. Rows of suspended timber pieces produce a sequence of tones that travels along the structure and out into the valley. Those who have been there recall how its sounds have joined the wind and distant cowbells which already move through the landscape. Called Le Bruit du Bois, or The Sound of Wood, the fifteen-square-meter installation was designed by Antoine Aunave, Flora Peyrot, Mathilde Steenhaut, and Luc Loviton for the 2026 Festival des Cabanes. The four ENSA Montpellier students won this year’s competition with the proposal, which was selected from close to 200 entries. The festival placed fourteen temporary structures around the Sources du Lac d’Annecy for its eleventh edition. images © Antoine Aunave nearly 1,000 timber chimes tune the valley The idea becomes clearest once someone starts moving along The Sound of Wood pavilion. The timber elements change in length across the structure to give each section a different sound. Running a stick through them sends a progression of tones down the wall. A single gesture turns the whole elevation into something closer to an oversized xylophone, with the surrounding valley acting as its acoustic room. There are close to 1,000 of these wooden chimes. Fabricating and installing them became a substantial part of the build for the young team, who worked with a group of fellow architecture students to construct the project on site. Their repetition gives the pavilion its visual character too. Seen from a distance, the pieces gather into a thin horizontal band against the steep terrain. Up close, the gaps between them let the landscape remain visible through the wall. the timber pavilion stretches horizontally across the steep alpine landscape a slender batten becomes structure and sound At the center of the design is a timber batten measuring just four centimeters across. The same slender profile is repeated through the pavilion, bending slightly as it rises and responding to the wind with small movements. The architects use this single dimension to build the structure and generate its sound, allowing a straightforward piece of milled timber to do much of the work. The pavilion sits above the uneven ground on an elevated walkway, with a handrail following one edge. Its asymmetrical frame stretches farther on the north side, guiding the approach before visitors move into the denser field of hanging pieces. Inside, the experience becomes more enclosed. Timber surrounds the body while openings between the chimes keep views toward the mountains and fields in reach. visitors can play Le Bruit du Bois by moving a wooden stick across its chimes architecture joins the existing sounds of the alps Sound gives the cabin a relationship with its setting that a framed view alone could hardly achieve. A visitor can set off a run of wooden tones, then let them fade back into the valley. At other moments, the breeze moves through the slender pieces on its own. The pavilion shifts between something people actively play and something that responds to the weather around it. It’s especially fitting for Le Festival des Cabanes, an architecture festival built around temporary interventions in the landscape around Lake Annecy. Here, the project asks visitors to listen as much as look. The satisfying part is how little machinery the effect requires. According to just- released estimates from market intelligence provider Apptopia , Muse’s app on mobile devices has been downloaded more times during its first 12 days on the market than ChatGPT was in the 12 days after its debut. (This data compares the U.S. and Canada markets only.) Muse also has more daily active users than ChatGPT had at the time, the firm found. Until now, it had been difficult to make an exact apples-to-apples comparison between these two apps, given that they had pursued different launch strategies. When ChatGPT arrived on mobile, it was made available globally, but only on iOS. Muse, meanwhile, is available across both Apple’s App Store and Google Play, but only in the U.S. and Canada. To better align the numbers for comparison, Apptopia looked only at the iOS data for the U.S. and Canada for both apps during the first 12 days of their respective launches. In this subset of the data, Muse has now seen 1.8 million downloads to ChatGPT’s 1.3 million. Overall, Muse has seen 2.8 million total installs globally in its first 12 days, the firm also said. Its growth hasn’t yet stagnated, either; Muse has moved up from its original position as No. 2 overall on the U.S. App Store immediately after its launch to now No. 1 , as Business Insider reported on Friday. That jump put the app higher than ChatGPT, the outlet noted. Another firm, Appfigures , said at the time that Muse had then crossed 1 million downloads. In addition, Apptopia’s data indicates that Muse’s U.S. daily active users are now higher than they were for ChatGPT at the same point after its launch. When comparing just the U.S. mobile app daily active users, Muse comes in higher with 642,000 daily users compared with 231,000 for ChatGPT at the time. To be fair to the fact that Muse is available across both iOS and Android, while ChatGPT launched on iOS only, Apptopia narrowed the comparison to iOS alone. See All by Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Paramount has reached a settlement with California and the 11 other states that sued to block its planned $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The settlement removes a major roadblock standing in the way of the massive media merger. According to the proposed consent decree filed with the court, it includes requirements like minimum numbers of theatrical film releases over the next five years, starting with 30 in year one and two, and 32 in the following years, and a commitment to spend at least $300 million more on production in the US compared to what the companies spent in 2025. At least four of the films produced must be independent films, and at least 20 percent must be “tentpole” blockbuster movies with $50 million-plus budgets, and releases on a minimum of 3,000 US screens within the first month. If Paramount doesn’t meet these film release requirements, it must divest Miramax Studios and pay $30 million per missed film. It also requires the merged company to keep offering a free streaming service, like Pluto TV, and includes a commitment not to sell Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years. The settlement has rules for the negotiations over cable channels owned by the combined company as well, in addition to requirements for a news editorial independence board “made up of five established journalists” with at least ten years of experience to ensure editorial independence at CBS and CNN. The Writers Guild of America also settled its antitrust lawsuit against Paramount At a press conference announcing the agreement, California AG Rob Bonta called the arrangement “the opposite” of the 2018 Disney-Fox deal , where Fox’s film output dropped afterward. “Let me be clear: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger,” Bonta adds in a press release . “But we believe this settlement, which resolves our antitrust concerns in every market alleged in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and puts workers’ needs, concerns, and futures first, is the best course of action.” Paramount Chairman & CEO David Ellison: We are grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, as well as the WGA, for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties, and to Governor Newsom for his support throughout this process. Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and — most importantly — the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling. We’re confident this agreement does exactly that, memorializing a series of commitments that include 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production to help revitalize our industry here at home. Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition. That vision was validated by unanimous approval from competition authorities in nearly 70 jurisdictions worldwide, who agreed this deal is pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker. Having now addressed the State AGs’ and WGA’s concerns, we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action. Bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery together will build that stronger Hollywood, creating expanded opportunity for our people and even more great entertainment for audiences around the world. The settlement comes just days before Paramount’s “ticking fee” was set to go into effect, which would require the entertainment giant to pay WBD shareholders 25 cents per share for each quarter the deal is delayed past September 30th. The fee would’ve cost Paramount about $7 million per day. Can Paramount break the Warner Bros. curse? Though the Trump administration signed off on the $110 billion merger, California, along with Arizona, Colorado, New York, Washington, and others, sued Paramount and WBD in July over antitrust concerns. They claimed the megamerger would create a “media behemoth” that would “inflict substantial harm” on the entertainment industry. According to the company’s updated IPO filing, Oura and its shareholders are together offering 50 million shares at a price range of $40 to $44 each. But most of the IPO’s proceeds will go to shareholders, who are offering 36.5 million shares, or almost two-thirds of the total. If the company lists at $42 per share, the midpoint of the price range, that would result in proceeds of about $1.53 billion for the shareholders and $567 million for the company, before fees and expenses. The bulk of that will go to Forerunner Ventures, the company’s second-largest shareholder. The venture firm plans to sell its entire 9.3% stake of about 28.7 million shares for about $1.20 billion (assuming the shares list at $42) before underwriting fees and taxes. Forerunner’s shares account for nearly 80% of the shares being sold by existing shareholders in the deal. Forerunner first invested in Oura in the company’s 2020 $28 million Series B round , according to PitchBook. Meanwhile, Oura doesn’t look to be treating this IPO as a fundraising event. At the $42 midpoint, the company expects net proceeds of $532.6 million and plans to use about $526.4 million to pay off accumulated tax obligations related to employee share grants that will vest at the time of the IPO. That would leave the company with roughly $6.2 million for general corporate purposes, according to the filing. In a way, this is kind of a flex by Oura, which is essentially using this IPO to give its early backers an exit. It’s also fulfilling tax obligations without turning to debt, as companies sometimes do, or touching its cash, which sat at about $372 million at the end of June.
